To do this, he uses a logical argument based on color, which is one of the accidents of a natural body.

“Either it belongs to the nature of a body to become colored, or it does not. If it belongs to its nature to become colored, then color must follow from the body’s own nature and is therefore the body’s own act. Something that follows from a thing’s own nature cannot at the same time depend on something else, just as what a thing acquires for itself cannot be the creation of another.
“But if it does not belong to the body’s nature to become colored, then God could color it and yet it might not become colored.”
In this final sentence, Muʿammar means that if color did not arise naturally from the body itself, it would have to come from God.

But that creates, in his view, an unacceptable possibility. God might will the body to become colored, while the body—because of a natural law—failed to become colored. What actually happened would then differ from what God had willed.
So according to his logical argument, color must arise from the natural activity of the body itself.
The same idea of generated action also appears in Muʿtazilite discussions of sensory perception among the Baghdad school.
One of its most important supporters was Bishr ibn al-Muʿtamir, the founder of the Baghdad Muʿtazilite school, who died in 226 AH/841 CE.
“A human being can produce perceptions through generation when he produces their causes.”
By “produces their causes,” we think he means that a person deliberately exposes his senses to sensible things. Sensation, or sensory perception, is then generated.

Sensation is therefore a generated act: a natural and involuntary event preceded by a voluntary cause, namely the person’s deliberate decision to expose the senses to something capable of producing sensation.
To sum up, this group of Muʿtazilites understands sensory knowledge as arising through two successive and connected stages.
First, the accidents of a body affect the senses.
Second, sensation—or sensory perception—is generated by that effect.

Both stages take place through necessary natural processes. But they may be preceded by a voluntary cause: the person deliberately exposing the senses to the qualities of natural bodies that can affect them.

Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf agrees with Muʿammar ibn ʿAbbād in distinguishing substance from accident, in accepting the existence of accidents, and in holding that accidents alone can be objects of sensory knowledge. Substances themselves, for both thinkers, can be known only through reason.
But al-ʿAllāf disagrees with Muʿammar’s explanation of sensory knowledge as a generated act ultimately attributable to the person who senses.
Here al-ʿAllāf takes a purely metaphysical position. He explains the transformation of sensible accidents into sensation, or sensory knowledge, as an act of God.
This is what we understand from the report of al-Ashʿarī, which is our only source for al-ʿAllāf’s position.

“Abū al-Hudhayl held that pleasure, color, tastes, smells, heat, cold, cowardice, courage, perception, and knowledge that arises in another person as a result of his action—all of these, according to Abū al-Hudhayl, are acts of God.”
At this point we need to return to al-Naẓẓām.

In al-Ashʿarī’s Maqālāt, we find a statement attributed to him that differs from the view of sensory knowledge we discussed earlier. In this statement, he combines Muʿammar’s idea that sensation is generated through a necessary natural process with al-ʿAllāf’s idea that sensation—the transformation of an external effect into sensory perception—comes about through divine action.
Al-Naẓẓām says here that both the movement of a stone as it falls or rises and the occurrence of perception are acts of God operating through a natural law.

A stone “moves when someone pushes it, falls when someone throws it downward, and rises when someone throws it upward. Perception is the same. All of this is an act of God through the necessity built into creation. This means that God gave the stone a nature such that, when someone pushes it, it moves. The same applies to all other generated things.”
This view agrees completely with the statement of al-Jāḥiẓ, al-Naẓẓām’s student, that all forms of knowledge arise necessarily through nature and that none of them are acts performed by human beings.
But if we accept this later statement from al-Naẓẓām, can we really say that it reconciles Muʿammar’s explanation of sensory knowledge with al-ʿAllāf’s?
It seems to us that al-Naẓẓām does not succeed in reconciling the two opposing views.
In fact, his solution conflicts with both.
On one side, it conflicts with Muʿammar, who completely rejects divine intervention in the production of perception.

On the other, it conflicts with al-ʿAllāf, who rejects the idea that any natural law stands between the effect of a sensible object and the sensation or perception that arises in a human being. Al-ʿAllāf makes that transformation an act of God alone.
We have seen where sensory knowledge begins in Muʿtazilite theory.
We now need to ask where it ends. In other words, how far can sensory knowledge take us in discovering the truths of the universe, the truth about God, and the nature of existence?
Our earlier discussion showed that the Muʿtazilites agree that sensory knowledge deals only with things that can be sensed—that is, with the material world.
This means that the senses reach their limit as soon as we confront realities whose objects are not material.
This is the starting point for the Muʿtazilite rejection of the idea that God can be seen with the eyes in the afterlife.
Their rejection follows from the first of their five principles: divine unity.
At its core, this principle rejects anything that would make God resemble material things.
Since sight perceives only colors and shapes, and colors and shapes are material, the Muʿtazilites unanimously deny that God can be seen with the eyes in the next world.
Abū al-Hudhayl and most Muʿtazilites nevertheless said: “We see God with our hearts, meaning that we know Him with our hearts.”
Here “knowledge” could mean rational knowledge or intuitive knowledge. Either way, it is not sensory knowledge.
But how can we know God through reason?
We will come to that question shortly.
For now, the conclusion is that sensory knowledge cannot, for the Muʿtazilites, provide a path to knowledge of God.
But why can it not provide a path to all other philosophical and cosmic truths—for example, the truth of existence, substances, and essences?
We can find the answer by returning to some of their arguments against seeing God with the eyes.
One of those arguments says that God is a pure substance, stripped of every accident—a simple and immaterial being.

Since substance itself cannot be seen with the eyes, they argue, God cannot be seen with the eyes either. To say otherwise would amount to attributing accidents to God, which they regard as impossible because it directly contradicts their claim that He is pure substance.
From this argument we can conclude that the senses, including sight, are also incapable of perceiving substances.
Their reason is that sight, for example, can be affected only by colors and shapes. But colors and shapes are accidents, not substances.
The same applies to the other senses.
Essences—what things are in themselves—are likewise simple, universal, and abstract. How, then, could the senses perceive them?
The same is true of “existence” when we mean existence in the universal and all-encompassing sense.
It follows that, for the Muʿtazilites, sensory knowledge cannot take us beyond the external world insofar as that world is made up of material things that can be sensed.

Yet although sensory knowledge cannot perceive what lies beyond the material and sensible, the Muʿtazilites still accept what the senses tell us within the material world. They treat sensory knowledge as a valid way of knowing that world.
At the same time, they also speak about the errors that often occur in sensation—what modern scientific language calls the deception of the senses.
Al-Naẓẓām, for example, says that bodies do not remain permanently the same but are renewed from moment to moment, even though the senses tell us otherwise.
He says of this: “The observer imagines that there is one single thing continuing unchanged.”

This is an acknowledgment that what actually happens in the material world—the constant renewal of bodies one after another—can differ from what the senses tell us, namely that bodies remain continuously the same.
Does this mean that al-Naẓẓām rejects the idea that sensory knowledge is a valid way of knowing the external world?
We have no direct statement from him that clearly answers this question.
Dr Albert Nasri Nader attributes to al-Naẓẓām the view that the error lies in the imagination rather than in sensation itself, because sensation cannot be wrong.
Dr Nader does not give a source for this claim. He may have inferred it from al-Naẓẓām’s statement that “the observer imagines…”—in particular, from the word “imagines.”
We doubt that al-Naẓẓām intended this meaning.

But even if we accept that the word can bear the meaning Dr Nader gives it, the first part of al-Naẓẓām’s statement says that “the senses judge otherwise.” Here al-Naẓẓām himself attributes the mistaken judgment to the senses, not to the imagination.

As for Dr Nader’s interpretation of this passage—that al-Naẓẓām means “the error of the senses here is an error in the whole, that is, in all judgments about particular things”—this reading likewise has no basis in al-Naẓẓām himself.

In any case, everything we have seen about sensory knowledge among the Muʿtazilites leads us back to the conclusion we reached earlier: in general, the Muʿtazilites accepted sensory knowledge as a valid way of knowing the external world.
By now it should be clear that the Muʿtazilites gave reason the highest place in the foundations of their system, and in the principles from which Muʿtazilite thought as a whole developed.

Their belief in human freedom of will is, at its core, one creative application of their basic view of reason. The same is true of the issue known in Muʿtazilite writings as “the question of rational good and evil,” which we will examine later in this study.

In fact, almost every question raised by the changing life of Arab-Islamic society in the Muʿtazilite period—whether it concerned doctrine, religious law, or human life—was approached by the Muʿtazilites through reason. They relied on reason to judge these questions, both in theory and in practice.

By now, this should be familiar enough that we do not need to spend much more time establishing it. What we need instead is to define, as far as the surviving Muʿtazilite sources allow us, what they meant by reason and by rational knowledge.
The first questions we face are these:
What is reason in Muʿtazilite theory? What does it do? And what are the limits of its ability to know?

The sources give us only a small number of passages in which the Muʿtazilites directly define reason. Even so, we can build up a broader picture from the many ways they apply reason when dealing with different problems.

The few direct definitions that have survived are concise and remarkably precise. They are enough to tell us a great deal. We also find many practical examples among Muʿtazilite thinkers, especially when they discuss things that cannot be known directly through the senses. These examples make it quite clear what they mean by reason, particularly when they speak about its role in knowledge.

We have two main definitions of reason before us. One comes from Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf, and the other from Abū ʿAlī Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb al-Jubbāʾī, a Basran Muʿtazilite who died in 303 AH/915 CE.
Al-Ashʿarī preserves al-ʿAllāf’s definition in three statements that complete one another and together form a single picture.

According to this definition, reason is “the power to acquire knowledge.” It is also “the power by which a person distinguishes himself from all other things.” And, he says, “we distinguish one thing from another through reason. We call sensory knowledge ‘reason’ only in the sense that it is something understood by reason.”

As we can see, this definition covers several things at once: what reason is capable of doing, how it works, what its role in knowledge actually is, what kinds of things it can know, and what kind of knowledge it produces.
First, reason is described as “the power to acquire knowledge.”
In Muʿtazilite terms, this means that reason can draw a universal idea from particular cases. As we have already seen, this is what the Muʿtazilites mean by knowledge.

If knowledge means discovering what a number of particular things of the same kind have in common, and then turning that shared feature into a general abstract concept, then reason is the power that allows a human being to make this discovery and carry out this transformation.
So this first part of the definition begins to tell us what reason does.
The second part takes us further. It says that reason is “the power by which a person distinguishes himself from all other things.”

This means, first, that a person becomes aware of himself. He then discovers what separates him from other things, and therefore what kind of relationship exists between the human self and the rest of existence.
